newsitem.title: CHINA: Hong Kong's "god of gambling" quits horseracing.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's "god of gambling" quits horseracing.

text.p: If you think money is one thing you can never ever get enough of, well, think again.
Professional punter Robert Moore, who has made hundreds of millions from Hong Kong's glitzy world of horseracing and carved an indelible mark in this super-capitalist city, is quitting.
"I've already made enough money, let other people do it," said the New Zealander, 44, who arrived in gambling-mad Hong Kong in 1989 to make his fortune punting on horses.
"I don't want to do it any more. I want to enjoy life more and I want to spend more time with my family and to slow down. Why should I keep going? I've got enough money."
Moore, revered locally as "the god of gambling", has been punting with the aid of computers and software which he developed and modified together with experts over the years.
At a news conference called to announce his retirement, Moore said gambling on the computer superhighway had become increasingly competitive in recent years.
"Computer generated gambling has increased at least tenfold since I arrived," he said. "Every year it gets harder to win because more people are learning how to do it properly.
"I'm quitting because it's getting harder and I don't want to take the risk of losing it," he said candidly.

A former golf caddie, Moore arrived in Hong Kong eight years ago with only A$5 (US$3.68) in his pocket. A friend bankrolled him HK$100,000 (US$12,900) and he turned it quickly into a HK$430,000 (US$55,600) win.
He now intends to sell his computer programme to the highest bidder, but has yet to give any estimate of the price.

Horseracing is part of the establishment in gambling-crazy Hong Kong. A huge industry, it outperforms some weighty blue chip companies in turnover. Money laid on a single race often exceeds the amount gambled on horses in many countries in an entire year.
But it is never straightforward. Dozens of people were arrested this year for race fixing in which some jockeys and horse trainers were alleged to be in cahoots with illegal bookmakers.
In his breezy manner, Moore, who owns a bar and a restaurant in Hong Kong, said he would concentrate on pool.

"I want to play pool and listen to music," he said, adding that he plans to open a night club in the Philippines. He is now married to a Hong Kong Chinese and has a 13-year-old daughter from a previous marriage.
